lines.text: In September, nineteen twenty-eight, Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to a cluttered lab bench.
On one forgotten dish, a mold had grown, and all around it, the bacteria had vanished.
That mold was leaking a substance that would save millions of lives. Its name? Penicillin.
So how does it kill germs, but leave us unharmed?
Zoom in on a bacterium. Its tough wall is a mesh of sugar chains, stitched together by tiny links.
To grow, the cell keeps loosening that mesh, while enzymes stitch in fresh links.
Penicillin mimics the end of those links. The enzymes grab it, and jam.
The cell keeps growing, but its wall can't keep up, until it bursts.
Human cells have no such wall, so the drug's target simply isn't there.
By the nineteen-forties, it was mass-produced, turning deadly infections into routine cures.
Not bad, for one messy bench.
